analysis.one_liner: Requires labels on milk from cows injected with synthetic growth hormone and lowers the price paid for that milk.
analysis.headline: The bill to require labels on milk from cows injected with synthetic growth hormone, introduced with 28 cosponsors (27 Democrats, 1 Republican), died in a House Agriculture subcommittee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every carton of milk or milk product from cows injected with synthetic bovine growth hormone (BGH) to say so, created a paper trail tracking who sells and injects the hormone, and set civil penalties up to $10,000 per violation. It also would have lowered the government-supported price paid for BGH milk so that federal dairy programs and non-using farms wouldn't absorb the cost of the extra milk supply, and it directed Health and Human Services to develop a test that could detect BGH residue and verify the labels.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, who would be able to tell at a glance whether their milk came from hormone-treated cows. Dairy farms that did not use the hormone would also gain: the bill's own findings cite Office of Management and Budget estimates that BGH use would cut overall dairy farm income by $1.3 billion over five years and add over $500 million in federal costs, and the price penalty is designed to shift those costs onto the farms that inject the hormone rather than onto taxpayers and the dairy market as a whole.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Milk buyers and farms not using the hormone

how_it_helps.text: Requires a plain-language label on milk and milk products from cows injected with synthetic BGH: "This milk was produced by cows injected with synthetic BGH," so shoppers can choose without relying on unregulated label claims that had already produced confusion and lawsuits.

Makes the labels enforceable: anyone who sells, buys, distributes, or injects synthetic BGH must keep records of where it went, and violations of the labeling or recordkeeping rules carry civil penalties of up to $10,000 per violation.

Amends the Agricultural Act of 1949 to lower the price received for BGH milk by the amount of the extra federal milk-purchase costs it causes, so farms that inject the hormone — not taxpayers and not farms that don't — cover the cost of the added surplus.

Directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to develop a scientifically valid residue test so BGH labels can actually be verified, and to make the test available to state agencies and dairy producers at the lowest possible cost.
Shields dairy farms that don't use the hormone from the income loss the bill's findings attribute to BGH adoption, citing an OMB estimate of a $1.3 billion drop in dairy farm income over five years.

analysis.who_pays: The manufacturers of synthetic BGH and the dairy farms and processors that use it: they would bear labeling and recordkeeping costs, exposure to civil penalties, and a lower price for their milk. Federal dairy and health agencies would also take on new labeling, records, and test-development work. Consumers would pay little or nothing directly.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hormone makers and farms that inject it

drawbacks.text: The FDA had already approved synthetic BGH as safe, and the bill's own findings concede this, describing the agency's determination that the hormone poses a "manageable risk" to consumers through increased antibiotic residues; the label mandate is therefore about information and choice, not proven harm, and critics could fairly call it stigmatizing for an approved product.

The price-reduction mechanism is blunt and hard to calibrate: USDA would have to calculate how much extra surplus and federal purchasing is attributable to BGH milk, and the penalty would push farms off the hormone through their pocketbooks rather than through any safety rule.

Labeling and recordkeeping impose real compliance costs and paperwork on dairies, processors, and the agencies that would administer the system, and the residue test the labels depend on did not yet exist, so enforcement would initially rest on paper records alone.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but informational: consumers get to know what is in a food staple their children drink, and non-adopting farms and taxpayers are protected from costs the bill's findings quantify in the billions. The costs fall on a concentrated group — one hormone's manufacturer and the farms that use it — in the form of labels, paperwork, penalties, and a lower milk price, for a product the government had approved as safe. The price-penalty mechanism is the weakest part: it is indirect, complicated to calculate, and functions as economic pressure rather than a food-safety standard. A well-designed version would have relied on labeling plus a verified residue test; the price cut rides along for farm-policy reasons.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Agriculture Committee and then to its dairy subcommittee, which never held a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Bernie Sanders introduced the Bovine Growth Hormone Milk Act on July 20, 1995 with 28 original cosponsors, nearly all Democrats.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Agriculture the day it was introduced, and a week later it was sent to the Subcommittee on Livestock, Dairy and Poultry.
No hearing, committee vote, or floor vote ever followed; the last recorded action was the subcommittee referral in July 1995, and the bill died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The manufacturer of synthetic BGH and the dairies that injected it came out ahead: no federal label requirement, no hormone paper trail, no penalties, and no price penalty ever took effect. Consumers never got the national labels the bill promised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The hormone's maker and dairies that used it

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 28 original cosponsors.

for.name: Christopher Shays
for.what_they_did: Was the bill's sole Republican cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: House Committee on Agriculture
against.role: Committee of referral, controlled by the Republican majority
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and never reported it out or scheduled any action on it.

against.name: Subcommittee on Livestock, Dairy and Poultry
against.role: House Agriculture subcommittee with jurisdiction over dairy
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 26, 1995 and held no hearing or vote for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Monsanto
against.role: Manufacturer of synthetic BGH (sold as Posilac)
against.what_they_did: Widely reported to have campaigned against mandatory labeling of milk from hormone-treated cows, which its product would have been subject to under the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Democratic — 27 of the 28 cosponsors were Democrats and one was a Republican — and the bill died in the Republican-controlled House Agriculture Committee without ever reaching a vote.

industries.note: The bill would have put a disclosure label on every carton of milk from treated cows, created a paper trail for every dose sold and injected, and cut the price received for BGH milk — a direct hit to the product's marketability and to the revenue of the company selling it. The bill's findings also cite cow health problems and increased antibiotic use that put the product's safety case in question.

Farms that injected the hormone would face labeling, recordkeeping, penalties, and a lower price for their milk, calibrated to the surplus costs their extra production causes federal dairy programs. Their interest in this bill ran against the consumers and non-using farms the bill serves.

industries.industry: Dairy farms not using synthetic BGH
industries.note: Non-adopting family farms would be shielded from the income loss the bill attributes to BGH-driven oversupply — a cited $1.3 billion drop in dairy farm income over five years — and would keep the option of marketing their milk as hormone-free without label wars.

Processors and stores would take on labeling and recordkeeping compliance costs, but non-treated milk lines would gain a clear, government-backed marketing edge. Some in this sector had already faced lawsuits over voluntary BGH labels, which the bill's findings cite.
